subject: biology

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the energy transformation that takes place in photosynthesis?
items.correct: Light energy absorbed by pigments is transformed into chemical energy in the carbon compounds made.
items.misconception: Energy is generated inside the chloroplast and then stored in glucose for the plant to use.
items.why: Everyday language says plants 'produce energy' and 'make their own food', and food is described as 'energy', so students picture the chloroplast as an energy factory rather than an energy converter. Photosynthesis is an energy transformation: light energy absorbed by pigments becomes chemical energy in the carbon compounds produced. The plant captures energy that already exists in sunlight; it creates none.
items.specStatementText: Light energy becomes chemical energy in carbon compounds
items.random_wrong: Light energy is converted into heat, which then speeds up the reactions that make glucose.

items.q: A fox eats a rabbit that has fed on grass. Where did the chemical energy in the carbon compounds of the fox's body originally come from?
items.correct: Light energy transformed into chemical energy by photosynthesis in the grass.
items.misconception: Chemical energy that the grass absorbed from the soil through its roots.
items.why: Fertilizer is sold as 'plant food', plants are watered and fed at the roots, and the idea that a tree's mass comes largely from an invisible gas is deeply counter-intuitive. The carbon compounds of a plant are built from carbon dioxide absorbed from the air, using light energy. The soil supplies water and mineral ions such as nitrate, but no carbon compounds and no energy.
items.specStatementText: Light energy becomes chemical energy in carbon compounds
items.random_wrong: New energy created by the grass in photosynthesis and passed on to the rabbit and fox.

items.q: Which word equation correctly summarises photosynthesis?
items.correct: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
items.misconception: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
items.why: The two word equations are taught side by side as mirror images, and students conclude that plants use one and animals the other, or reverse the equation when recalling it. Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and water and produces glucose and oxygen using light energy. Cell respiration, which plants also carry out continuously, releases energy from glucose. The equations describe different processes in different organelles.
items.specStatementText: Carbon dioxide plus water gives glucose, with water supplying the hydrogen
items.random_wrong: carbon dioxide + light energy → glucose + oxygen

items.q: Glucose produced by photosynthesis contains hydrogen atoms. From which substance were these hydrogen atoms obtained?
items.correct: Water molecules, which are split during photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide molecules joined together to make glucose.
items.why: Students know that all cells need water, so they treat it as a background requirement rather than as a chemical that is broken apart; and 'carbon dioxide is converted to glucose' sounds as if carbon dioxide alone is enough. Glucose (C6H12O6) contains hydrogen that carbon dioxide cannot supply. Water is split during photosynthesis to provide this hydrogen; the oxygen left over is released. Water is therefore a genuine reactant.
items.specStatementText: Carbon dioxide plus water gives glucose, with water supplying the hydrogen
items.random_wrong: Mineral ions the roots absorbed from the soil water.

items.q: Algae were supplied with water containing the heavy isotope oxygen-18 and ordinary carbon dioxide; the oxygen gas they released contained oxygen-18. Other algae were given ordinary water and carbon dioxide containing oxygen-18; the oxygen gas they released contained no oxygen-18. What do these results show?
items.correct: The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water and not from carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: The oxygen released comes from carbon dioxide once its carbon has been removed to make glucose.
items.why: Carbon dioxide contains oxygen, and 'plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen' makes the exchange look like a simple swap of one gas for another. The oxygen produced by photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water, as experiments with the isotope oxygen-18 showed. The oxygen atoms of carbon dioxide end up in glucose and in water, not in the oxygen released.
items.specStatementText: Oxygen is left over from splitting water
items.random_wrong: Water is not a reactant but only dissolves the carbon dioxide before the reaction takes place.

items.q: Which list includes all of the groups of organisms that release oxygen as a by-product of photosynthesis?
items.correct: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria
items.misconception: Plants, algae, cyanobacteria, fungi
items.why: Fungi were classified as plants historically, grow in soil, and are still called 'plants' in everyday speech. Oxygen is released by photosynthesis in plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Fungi belong to a separate kingdom, contain no chlorophyll, and obtain their carbon compounds by digesting and absorbing organic matter.
items.specStatementText: Oxygen is left over from splitting water
items.random_wrong: Plants and algae, no bacteria

items.q: On a paper chromatogram of leaf pigments, the origin line was 20 mm from the bottom edge of the paper, the centre of the carotene spot was 65 mm from the bottom edge and the solvent front was 70 mm from the bottom edge. What is the Rf value of carotene?
items.why: The paper does dip into the solvent at its bottom edge, so students take the edge as the starting point instead of the origin line above it. Both the pigment and the solvent start from the origin line, so both distances are measured from that line. Measuring from the paper edge adds the same extra length to both and gives an Rf that is too high.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography separates pigments, and Rf identifies them

items.q: In the solvent used, reference Rf values for leaf pigments are: carotene 0.95 (orange), xanthophyll 0.71 (yellow), chlorophyll a 0.65 (blue-green) and chlorophyll b 0.45 (yellow-green). A student's chromatogram shows three spots: orange at Rf 0.94, blue-green at Rf 0.66 and yellow-green at Rf 0.44. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: The extract contains carotene, chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b; any xanthophyll was too faint to see.
items.misconception: The extract contains only chlorophyll, which the solvent has separated into three coloured forms.
items.why: Students learn 'chlorophyll' as a singular word and the leaf looks uniformly green, so the yellow and orange pigments are masked both visually and in the vocabulary. Green leaves contain a mixture of pigments. Chromatography separates them into spots of different colours (blue-green chlorophyll a, yellow-green chlorophyll b, yellow xanthophylls, orange carotene) that are identified by colour and Rf value.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography separates pigments, and Rf identifies them
items.random_wrong: The Rf values differ from the reference values, so none of the three pigments can be identified reliably.

items.q: A chlorophyll molecule in a leaf absorbs a photon of red light. What happens within the molecule as a result?
items.correct: An electron is raised to a higher energy level.
items.misconception: It vibrates faster, warming the surrounding stroma.
items.why: Objects left in sunlight get hot, and students have met 'energy' in biology mostly as heat, so heating is the only mechanism they can picture for using light. Absorbing a photon excites an electron within the pigment molecule. The energy of the excited electron, not heat, is what is transformed into chemical energy in ATP and reduced NADP and ultimately in carbon compounds.
items.specStatementText: Pigments absorb only certain wavelengths, exciting electrons
items.random_wrong: It splits a molecule of water that is bound to it.

items.q: The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a has peaks at about 430 nm (blue) and 660 nm (red) but a trough at about 550 nm (green). Which statement best explains this pattern?
items.correct: Only photons whose energy matches that needed to excite an electron in chlorophyll a are absorbed; blue and red photons match, green do not.
items.misconception: Green photons carry too little energy to excite an electron in chlorophyll a, whereas blue and red photons both carry more than enough energy to do so.
items.why: Students carry over a 'more energy is better' picture, or the threshold idea from the photoelectric effect in physics, and expect any sufficiently energetic photon to be taken up. Electron energy levels are discrete, so the photon's energy must match the gap between levels. Red photons (lower energy) are absorbed by chlorophyll while green photons (higher energy than red) are not, which shows that absorption depends on matching, not on exceeding a threshold.
items.specStatementText: Pigments absorb only certain wavelengths, exciting electrons
items.random_wrong: Chlorophyll a absorbs green light more strongly than any other colour, which is exactly why leaves that contain it appear green.

items.q: Samples of an aquatic plant were exposed to light of different wavelengths and the oxygen produced was collected: at 450 nm, 12 cm³ in 10 minutes; at 550 nm, 6 cm³ in 15 minutes; at 650 nm, 15 cm³ in 15 minutes; at 700 nm, 3 cm³ in 5 minutes. Which statement about the action spectrum plotted from these data is correct?
items.correct: The highest rate is at 450 nm, at 1.2 cm³ of oxygen produced per minute.
items.misconception: The highest rate is at 650 nm, because that sample produced the most oxygen.
items.why: Students treat 'rate' and 'amount' as synonyms, and in many school practicals every sample runs for the same time so the distinction never matters. Rate = amount ÷ time. To determine rates of photosynthesis from data for oxygen production or carbon dioxide consumption, each amount must be divided by the time over which it was measured before the wavelengths are compared or plotted as an action spectrum.
items.specStatementText: Absorption spectra and action spectra look alike but measure different things
items.random_wrong: The rate at 550 nm should be plotted as zero, because chlorophyll reflects green.

items.q: Pure chlorophyll a absorbs very little light at 550 nm (green), yet the action spectrum of a whole leaf shows a rate of photosynthesis at 550 nm of about 30% of the maximum. Which explanation is best?
items.correct: Accessory pigments absorb some of the green light that chlorophyll a does not, and pass the energy on.
items.misconception: The reading must be an error, because leaves reflect green light and so cannot photosynthesize in it at all.
items.why: 'Chlorophyll reflects green light' is taught as the reason leaves are green, and students turn 'absorbs little' into 'absorbs none'. The action spectrum shows a trough in the green region but not zero. Accessory pigments such as chlorophyll b and carotenoids absorb some of the wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and pass the energy on, which is one reason the action spectrum is broader than the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a.
items.specStatementText: Absorption spectra and action spectra look alike but measure different things
items.random_wrong: In a living leaf chlorophyll a absorbs green light strongly, which is the reason the leaf appears green to the eye.

items.q: A student places a lamp at different distances from a beaker of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution kept at 25 °C, and counts the bubbles of gas released per minute at each distance. Which correctly identifies the variables?
items.correct: Independent: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
items.misconception: Independent: bubbles per minute; dependent: distance of lamp
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'depends on' points the wrong way: students reason that the outcome depends on light, so light is 'dependent'. The independent variable is the one deliberately changed by the investigator (light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature); the dependent variable is the one measured to see the effect (the rate of photosynthesis).
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.random_wrong: Controlled variable: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute

items.q: Pondweed submerged in water at 25 °C with the carbon dioxide concentration of ordinary air was exposed to increasing light intensity. The rate of photosynthesis rose at first and then levelled off, staying constant however much the light intensity was increased. Which change is most likely to raise the rate at this plateau?
items.correct: Adding sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water to raise the carbon dioxide concentration.
items.misconception: Moving the lamp even closer, so that the light intensity becomes higher still.
items.why: Students generalise from the rising part of the graph and expect a straight-line relationship, and everyday experience suggests that a brighter day means more growth. The rate is set by whichever factor is in shortest supply. When light is plentiful, another factor limits the rate and increasing light intensity further has no effect; the graph shows a plateau.
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.random_wrong: Nothing, because the plateau is the maximum rate of which the plant is capable.

items.q: Tomato plants were grown in two enclosed greenhouses, one at 400 ppm carbon dioxide and one at 800 ppm. Both were kept at 22 °C with the same lighting and watering, and after six weeks the dry mass of the plants was measured. Which is a controlled variable in this experiment?
items.correct: The temperature of 22 °C in both greenhouses
items.misconception: The carbon dioxide concentration in the greenhouses
items.why: In everyday speech, to control something is to decide its value, and the experimenter does decide the value of the independent variable. In experimental design 'controlled' means held constant. The variable that is deliberately varied (carbon dioxide concentration) is the independent variable; temperature, light and water supply that are kept the same are the controlled variables.
items.specStatementText: Growing plants in extra carbon dioxide to predict the future
items.random_wrong: The dry mass of the plants measured at six weeks

items.q: In an enclosed greenhouse trial, wheat grown at 550 ppm carbon dioxide gave 35% more grain than wheat at 370 ppm. In a FACE experiment with the same variety in open fields, plots at 550 ppm gave 13% more grain than plots at 370 ppm. Which is the best explanation of the difference?
items.correct: Other factors, such as water and nitrogen supply, also limit growth in the field, so the extra carbon dioxide gives a smaller gain.
items.misconception: The response of a variety to carbon dioxide is a fixed property of that variety, so the FACE plots must in fact have received less than 550 ppm carbon dioxide.
items.why: Students learn the Calvin cycle as a universal pathway and assume a universal pathway must give a universal response, forgetting that growth in the field is limited by water, nutrients, pests and weather as well as by carbon dioxide. Greenhouse experiments give precise control but idealised conditions. Field experiments in natural ecosystems or crops include the other limiting factors, which is why FACE is needed to predict future rates of photosynthesis and plant growth realistically.
items.specStatementText: Growing plants in extra carbon dioxide to predict the future
items.random_wrong: The FACE result is unreliable because weather and soil could not be held constant, so only the greenhouse figure should be used to predict future yields.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes a photosystem?
items.correct: An array of chlorophyll and accessory pigments held in a membrane, with a special chlorophyll at the reaction centre that emits an excited electron.
items.misconception: A single chlorophyll molecule that absorbs light by itself and carries out the whole of the light-dependent reactions on its own.
items.why: 'Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis' is the whole story at GCSE and MYP, and diagrams of the chloroplast show chlorophyll as scattered green dots. Photosystems are molecular arrays of chlorophyll and accessory pigments held in a membrane. Most of the pigments only absorb light and pass the energy on; a special chlorophyll at the reaction centre is the one that emits an excited electron.
items.specStatementText: A photosystem is an array of pigments around one reaction centre
items.random_wrong: A cluster of pigment molecules dissolved in the stroma, from which excited electrons pass across into the thylakoid space.

items.q: Cyanobacteria carry out photosynthesis using photosystems similar to those of plants. Where are the photosystems of a cyanobacterium located?
items.correct: In membranes inside the cell, because cyanobacteria are prokaryotes with no chloroplasts.
items.misconception: In the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts that cyanobacteria contain, as in plant cells.
items.why: The chloroplast is taught as 'the site of photosynthesis', so students assume that anything photosynthetic must contain one. Photosystems are always located in membranes. In photosynthetic eukaryotes these are the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts; in cyanobacteria, which are prokaryotes without membrane-bound organelles, they are membranes within the cell itself.
items.specStatementText: A photosystem is an array of pigments around one reaction centre
items.random_wrong: Free in the cytoplasm, dissolved in the fluid that surrounds the DNA of the cell.

items.q: Why is a structured array of many different pigment molecules, rather than a single chlorophyll molecule, needed to carry out the first step of photosynthesis?
items.correct: Different pigments absorb a wide range of wavelengths and funnel the energy to one reaction centre, which is excited far more often than a lone molecule.
items.misconception: The accessory pigments only protect the chlorophyll from damage by bright light; a single chlorophyll could absorb the light equally well by itself.
items.why: Carotenoids are sometimes introduced as 'protective' pigments, and students take that as their only function. The advantage of having different types of pigment in the structured array is that between them they absorb a wider range of wavelengths and funnel the energy to a single reaction centre. A single molecule of chlorophyll or any other pigment could not perform any part of photosynthesis on its own.
items.specStatementText: Why an array beats a single pigment molecule
items.random_wrong: Each pigment molecule in the array carries out photosynthesis by itself, so the array simply packs more independent working units into the thylakoid membrane.

items.q: Which statement about the photolysis of water in photosystem II is correct?
items.correct: Its electrons replace those lost by the reaction centre, its protons join the gradient and oxygen is waste.
items.misconception: Light absorbed directly by water molecules in the thylakoid lumen breaks them apart into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
items.why: The word 'photolysis' literally means splitting by light, and students take it literally. Water is not split by light itself. Light excites the reaction centre of photosystem II, which loses an electron and becomes a strong oxidizing agent that takes electrons from water, releasing protons and oxygen.
items.specStatementText: Photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen
items.random_wrong: The hydrogen released from water is passed straight to NADP at photosystem II, reducing it before the electrons move on.

items.q: Photolysis of water by cyanobacteria began releasing oxygen into the oceans and atmosphere more than two billion years ago. Which statement describes a consequence of this?
items.correct: Oxygen oxidized dissolved iron, forming banded iron formations in rocks, and was toxic to many of the anaerobic organisms living at the time.
items.misconception: Oxygen benefited all the organisms living at the time, because every one of them was able to switch from anaerobic to aerobic respiration.
items.why: Students know oxygen as essential to their own life and assume it has always been beneficial to every organism. Free oxygen is a reactive, toxic gas for organisms without protective enzymes. Its accumulation, produced by photolysis in cyanobacteria, had immense consequences: it killed many anaerobes, oxidized dissolved iron to form banded iron formations, and eventually made aerobic respiration and the ozone layer possible.
items.specStatementText: Photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen
items.random_wrong: Oxygen levels did not rise until land plants evolved, because bacteria release too little oxygen to affect the atmosphere.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes how ATP is produced in the thylakoid?
items.correct: Electron carriers pump protons into the thylakoid lumen, and the protons flow back into the stroma through ATP synthase, which makes ATP.
items.misconception: The electron carriers make ATP directly as electrons pass along them, transferring the energy of each electron into a phosphate bond on ADP.
items.why: Diagrams place the electron transport chain next to ATP, and students have met substrate-level phosphorylation where a reaction does make ATP directly. ATP production in thylakoids is by chemiosmosis: the electron carriers pump protons to build a gradient across the thylakoid membrane, and ATP synthase converts the energy of that gradient into ATP.
items.specStatementText: Chemiosmosis in thylakoids makes ATP
items.random_wrong: Protons are pumped out of the lumen into the stroma and flow back into the lumen through ATP synthase, releasing ATP inside it.

items.q: A herbicide blocks the flow of electrons out of photosystem II. Chloroplasts treated with it are kept in bright light with a supply of ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which process can continue?
items.correct: ATP production by cyclic photophosphorylation, since photosystem I can still emit electrons that return to it via the carriers.
items.misconception: Continuous reduction of NADP, because photosystem I generates its own electrons from light and so needs no supply from elsewhere.
items.why: The guide says photosystems 'generate and emit excited electrons', and students read 'generate' as 'create from nothing'. A photosystem generates an excited electron by raising the energy of one of its own electrons. Once it is emitted the reaction centre is left positively charged and cannot emit again until the electron is replaced, which is why photosystem II must split water and photosystem I depends on electrons arriving from the carriers.
items.specStatementText: Chemiosmosis in thylakoids makes ATP
items.random_wrong: Oxygen release, because light continues to split water molecules directly whether or not photosystem II passes on its electrons.

items.q: A chemical is added that makes the thylakoid membrane freely permeable to protons, so that no proton gradient can build up across it. The chloroplasts are illuminated with a supply of ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which prediction is correct?
items.correct: Oxygen and reduced NADP continue to be produced in the light, but ATP synthesis stops completely.
items.misconception: Everything stops, because without ATP the photosystems have no energy to emit electrons.
items.why: Students learn that ATP powers cell processes and apply the rule universally, without noticing that here ATP is being made rather than used. In the light-dependent reactions the energy flows from light to excited electrons to a proton gradient to ATP. Electron transport does not depend on ATP being made: if an uncoupler dissipates the proton gradient, ATP synthesis stops but electrons continue to flow and NADP continues to be reduced.
items.specStatementText: Chemiosmosis in thylakoids makes ATP
items.random_wrong: ATP is still made, because the electron carriers phosphorylate ADP directly as the electrons pass along.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the reduction of NADP in the light-dependent reactions?
items.correct: NADP accepts two electrons that have come from photosystem I and a hydrogen ion from the stroma, forming reduced NADP.
items.misconception: NADP accepts hydrogen atoms that are released directly by the splitting of water at photosystem II, forming reduced NADP.
items.why: The SL statement says hydrogen is 'obtained by splitting water', so students connect the water-splitting site directly to the hydrogen carrier. The electrons from water pass along the whole chain, through photosystem I, before reaching NADP. NADP accepts two electrons from photosystem I and one hydrogen ion from the stroma, forming reduced NADP.
items.specStatementText: Photosystem I reduces NADP
items.random_wrong: NADP accepts electrons that are returning to photosystem I in cyclic photophosphorylation, forming reduced NADP.

items.q: What happens to reduced NADP after it has been formed by photosystem I?
items.correct: It carries electrons and hydrogen into the stroma, where they reduce glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate.
items.misconception: It passes its electrons to the chain of carriers so that protons are pumped, as reduced NAD does in mitochondria.
items.why: Students have just learned that reduced NAD from glycolysis and the Krebs cycle donates electrons to the mitochondrial chain, and assume the similarly named reduced NADP does the same. In photosynthesis the electron flow runs the other way: the chain reduces NADP as its final step. Reduced NADP is the product of the light-dependent reactions and is consumed in the stroma by the light-independent reactions.
items.specStatementText: Photosystem I reduces NADP
items.random_wrong: It supplies the phosphate and energy needed to convert triose phosphate back into RuBP in the stroma.

items.q: Which statement correctly locates the light-dependent reactions within a thylakoid?
items.correct: Water is split on the lumen side of photosystem II, ATP synthase releases ATP into the stroma and NADP is reduced on the stroma side.
items.misconception: Water is split in the stroma, and ATP and reduced NADP are made in the thylakoid lumen, where the enzymes of the Calvin cycle then use them.
items.why: Both compartment names are new and unfamiliar, and students learn the pair of locations without a reason to attach each to its process. Photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase are membrane proteins, so the light-dependent reactions are in the thylakoid membrane: photolysis on the lumen side, ATP released into the stroma, NADP reduced on the stroma side. The soluble enzymes of the Calvin cycle, including Rubisco, are in the stroma.
items.specStatementText: Where each light-dependent reaction happens in a thylakoid
items.random_wrong: Protons are pumped out into the stroma, and ATP synthase makes ATP inside the thylakoid lumen as the protons flow back in across the membrane.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes carbon fixation by Rubisco?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP, forming two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP to form a six-carbon sugar, which is then released as glucose.
items.why: Glucose is the product of the word equation, and a five-carbon molecule plus one carbon does add up to six, so students assume the six-carbon compound is glucose. The six-carbon compound formed is unstable and immediately splits into two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate. Glucose is made much later from triose phosphate that leaves the cycle.
items.specStatementText: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP
items.random_wrong: Rubisco uses the energy of ATP to attach carbon dioxide to RuBP, forming glycerate 3-phosphate.

items.q: Rubisco can make up half of the soluble protein in a leaf and is the most abundant enzyme on Earth. Which explanation of this abundance is best?
items.correct: It catalyses each reaction relatively slowly and is not effective at low carbon dioxide concentrations, so many molecules are needed.
items.misconception: It is an exceptionally fast and efficient enzyme with a high affinity for carbon dioxide, so plants invest heavily in it.
items.why: Students associate abundance with importance and importance with excellence, and cannot see why a cell would make huge amounts of a poor enzyme. Rubisco catalyses only a few reactions per second and has a low affinity for carbon dioxide, which is present at only about 0.04% in air. The plant compensates for a slow, inefficient enzyme by making enormous quantities of it.
items.specStatementText: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP
items.random_wrong: It is used up each time it fixes a molecule of carbon dioxide, so large amounts must be made continuously to replace what is lost.

items.q: What is required to convert glycerate 3-phosphate into triose phosphate in the Calvin cycle?
items.correct: ATP, which phosphorylates glycerate 3-phosphate, and reduced NADP, which reduces it.
items.misconception: ATP only; the reduced NADP is saved for the later regeneration of RuBP from triose phosphate.
items.why: Students remember that there are two products of the light-dependent reactions and two energy-requiring stages, and pair them one to one rather than learning which step needs what. The reduction of glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate uses ATP (to phosphorylate) and reduced NADP (to reduce). Regenerating RuBP from triose phosphate uses ATP only; reduced NADP has no role there.
items.specStatementText: Glycerate 3-phosphate is reduced to triose phosphate
items.random_wrong: Reduced NADP only; ATP from the light-dependent reactions is not used in the light-independent reactions.

items.q: In a Calvin cycle that produces one molecule of glucose, how many molecules of triose phosphate are made in total, and how many of them are used to regenerate RuBP?
items.correct: 12 made, 10 recycled
items.misconception: 12 made, 6 recycled
items.why: Diagrams of a single turn show two glycerate 3-phosphates becoming two triose phosphates, and students assume the pair divides evenly between the two fates. Regenerating three RuBP (15 carbons) needs five triose phosphates (15 carbons). Only every sixth triose phosphate can be spared, so five-sixths of all triose phosphate produced must be converted back to RuBP if glucose is the product.
items.specStatementText: Five triose phosphates rebuild three RuBP
items.random_wrong: 6 made, 5 recycled

items.q: What is required for the conversion of five molecules of triose phosphate into three molecules of RuBP?
items.correct: ATP from the light-dependent reactions, but no reduced NADP
items.misconception: No ATP and no reduced NADP, because the reactions are spontaneous
items.why: Students learn that ATP and reduced NADP are used 'to make triose phosphate' and treat the rest of the cycle as free. Converting five triose phosphates into three RuBP requires ATP; RuBP carries two phosphate groups and the second is added using ATP. Without ATP the cycle cannot continue.
items.specStatementText: Five triose phosphates rebuild three RuBP
items.random_wrong: Both ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions

items.q: A plant makes the amino acid alanine, which contains carbon and nitrogen. Where do these atoms come from?
items.correct: The carbon is fixed in the Calvin cycle and the nitrogen comes from nitrate or ammonium absorbed by the roots.
items.misconception: The whole amino acid is absorbed from the soil, where decomposers have released it from dead organisms.
items.why: Glucose is the only product named in the word equation, and fertilizer and compost are described as 'feeding' the plant. All the carbon in the compounds of a photosynthesizing organism is fixed in the Calvin cycle. Carbon compounds other than glucose are made by metabolic pathways that branch from an intermediate of the cycle; mineral nutrients such as nitrate supply other elements but no carbon.
items.specStatementText: Every carbon compound in the plant traces back to the Calvin cycle
items.random_wrong: Both are fixed in the Calvin cycle, which fixes nitrogen gas from the air as well as carbon dioxide.

items.q: Algae photosynthesizing steadily in light with a plentiful supply of carbon dioxide are suddenly placed in darkness. Within a minute the concentration of glycerate 3-phosphate in the cells rises sharply. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: No ATP or reduced NADP is being made, so glycerate 3-phosphate cannot be reduced, while Rubisco continues to fix carbon dioxide for a time.
items.misconception: The light-independent reactions actually run faster in darkness, so glycerate 3-phosphate is produced much more quickly than it can be used up.
items.why: The older name 'dark reactions', and the phrase 'light-independent', suggest to students that darkness is when these reactions occur. 'Light-independent' means that light is not used directly. The reactions depend entirely on ATP and reduced NADP supplied by the light-dependent reactions, so they run in the light and cease soon after light is removed.
items.specStatementText: Each set of reactions depends on the other
items.random_wrong: Reduced NADP is diverted to the chain of electron carriers to make ATP, so none of it remains to reduce glycerate 3-phosphate.

items.q: Illuminated chloroplasts are deprived of carbon dioxide. Photosystem II soon stops emitting electrons. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The Calvin cycle stops using ATP and reduced NADP, so NADP and ADP are not regenerated; electrons cannot leave photosystem I and the chain backs up to photosystem II.
items.misconception: Only the Calvin cycle is affected; the light-dependent reactions continue at their full rate and store up ATP and reduced NADP for later use.
items.why: The two stages are taught as separate and sequential, so students see the light-dependent reactions as an independent supplier that is unaffected by demand. The stages are interdependent. The light-dependent reactions need NADP and ADP returned from the Calvin cycle. When carbon dioxide is lacking, reduced NADP accumulates and no NADP is available to accept electrons, so electrons back up along the chain and photosystem II cannot emit or replace electrons.
items.specStatementText: Each set of reactions depends on the other
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide is the molecule split by photosystem II to obtain its electrons and oxygen, so without it there is no source of electrons.

items.q: A student notices that pondweed in a tank of hydrogencarbonate solution at 30 °C releases bubbles of gas faster than identical pondweed in the same solution at 15 °C under the same lamp. Which is the most appropriate hypothesis to test in a follow-up experiment?
items.correct: Between 15 °C and 30 °C, raising the temperature increases the rate of photosynthesis because its enzyme-catalysed reactions run faster.
items.misconception: Photosynthesis is faster at 30 °C than at 15 °C, and the observation has already proven this, so no further experiment is needed.
items.why: Students meet 'proof' in mathematics, where a single valid argument settles the matter, and apply the same standard to an experiment. A single experiment can support or refute a hypothesis but cannot prove it. Hypotheses in science are provisional explanations that require repeated testing, and a supported hypothesis remains open to revision.
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.random_wrong: Heat energy from the warmer water is what drives the reactions of photosynthesis, so the pondweed at 30 °C has more energy to use.

items.q: A leaf sealed in a chamber was illuminated with light of one wavelength at a time and the fall in carbon dioxide concentration in the chamber was recorded: at 450 nm the concentration fell by 80 ppm in 4 minutes; at 550 nm by 30 ppm in 5 minutes; at 650 nm by 90 ppm in 6 minutes; at 700 nm by 20 ppm in 2 minutes. Which statement about these results is correct?
items.correct: The highest rate is at 450 nm, because carbon dioxide was consumed there at 20 ppm per minute.
items.misconception: The results give an absorption spectrum of the leaf pigments, not an action spectrum.
items.why: The two graphs have a similar shape with peaks in blue and red and are often drawn on the same axes, so students do not notice that the vertical axes measure different things. An absorption spectrum is a property of a pigment, measured with a spectrophotometer. An action spectrum is a property of a photosynthesizing organism, obtained by measuring oxygen production or carbon dioxide consumption at each wavelength. Their similar shape is evidence that the absorbed light drives photosynthesis.
items.specStatementText: Absorption spectra and action spectra look alike but measure different things
items.random_wrong: The highest rate is at 650 nm, because the largest fall in carbon dioxide occurred there.

items.q: What is the useful product of photosynthesis for the organism that carries it out?
items.correct: The carbon compounds, such as glucose, which hold chemical energy; oxygen is a by-product.
items.misconception: The purpose of photosynthesis is to make oxygen, so oxygen is the main product and the sugar is a side effect.
items.why: From primary school onwards, students are taught that plants are important because they 'give us oxygen', so oxygen becomes the product they remember and value. Oxygen is a by-product formed when water is split to obtain hydrogen. The photosynthesizing cell gains nothing from it and releases it; the useful products are the carbon compounds in which the transformed energy is stored.
items.specStatementText: Oxygen is left over from splitting water
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which organisms release oxygen by photosynthesis?
items.correct: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria; cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, so photosynthesis is not restricted to eukaryotes.
items.misconception: Only green plants (and perhaps algae) photosynthesize; bacteria cannot, because bacteria are decomposers or pathogens.
items.why: GCSE and MYP courses attribute photosynthesis to 'green plants and algae', and bacteria are met almost entirely as agents of decay and disease. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes that split water and release oxygen, just as plants and algae do, using photosystems held in membranes inside the cell. They were the first organisms to release oxygen into the atmosphere.
items.specStatementText: Oxygen is left over from splitting water
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is an Rf value calculated?
items.correct: Distance moved by the pigment from the origin divided by distance moved by the solvent front from the origin, giving a value between 0 and 1.
items.misconception: Rf is the solvent distance divided by the pigment distance, so it is the larger number over the smaller.
items.why: Students are used to dividing the larger quantity by the smaller to get a 'sensible' answer greater than one, and the two distances are both measured from the same origin so their order is easily swapped. Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. Because a pigment can never move further than the solvent that carries it, Rf is always between 0 and 1; a value above 1 shows the ratio has been inverted.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography separates pigments, and Rf identifies them
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an Rf value be used to identify a pigment?
items.correct: Yes. For a given pigment, solvent and stationary phase the Rf is constant, so it can be compared with reference values.
items.misconception: Rf values change from one chromatogram to the next depending on how far the solvent ran, so they cannot reliably identify a pigment.
items.why: The distances themselves do differ every time a chromatogram is run, and students who have not internalised that Rf is a ratio expect the ratio to vary too. Because the pigment and the solvent travel for the same time in the same medium, the ratio of their distances is constant however long the strip or the run. Small differences from reference values reflect measurement uncertainty, not a different pigment.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography separates pigments, and Rf identifies them
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which colours of light does chlorophyll absorb?
items.correct: Mainly blue and red; green light is absorbed poorly and is reflected or transmitted, which is why leaves look green.
items.misconception: Chlorophyll absorbs green light, because leaves are green and a pigment must absorb the colour it shows.
items.why: Everyday intuition links the colour of an object with what it 'takes in'; students have not been taught that the colour seen is the light that is reflected rather than absorbed. The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll has peaks in the blue and red regions and a trough in the green. The green light that is not absorbed is reflected or transmitted, giving leaves their colour.
items.specStatementText: Pigments absorb only certain wavelengths, exciting electrons
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is water supply investigated as a limiting factor of photosynthesis?
items.correct: No. The limiting factors investigated are carbon dioxide concentration, light intensity and temperature; water supply rarely limits photosynthesis directly and is not varied experimentally.
items.misconception: Water is a limiting factor of photosynthesis in the same way as carbon dioxide, because it is a reactant in the word equation.
items.why: Water appears as a reactant in the equation, so students assume that adding water must speed up the reaction, just as adding carbon dioxide does. Only a tiny fraction of the water a plant absorbs is used in photosynthesis, and a submerged aquatic plant is surrounded by water. Before water shortage limits photolysis, the plant wilts and closes its stomata, which limits carbon dioxide instead. The factors varied experimentally are carbon dioxide, light and temperature.
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the plateau on a graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity represent?
items.correct: The rate at which some other factor has become limiting; raising that factor would raise the plateau.
items.misconception: The plateau is the maximum rate of which the plant is capable, an intrinsic ceiling that no change in conditions can raise.
items.why: The graph looks as if it has reached a top, and students read the flat line as 'the plant is going as fast as it can'. The plateau shows that light is no longer the limiting factor. Increasing the carbon dioxide concentration (or the temperature, if that is limiting) raises the rate to a new, higher plateau.
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is a controlled variable?
items.correct: A variable that could affect the result and is kept constant across all treatments.
items.misconception: The controlled variable is the control group, such as the plots or plants that receive no extra carbon dioxide.
items.why: 'Control' is used for two different ideas, the control treatment and the controlled variables, and students merge them because the words look the same. A control treatment (for example plots at ambient carbon dioxide) provides a comparison. Controlled variables are factors such as temperature, light and watering that are kept the same for every treatment so that they cannot cause the difference in results.
items.specStatementText: Growing plants in extra carbon dioxide to predict the future
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are photosystems dissolved in the stroma of the chloroplast?
items.correct: No. Photosystems are always located in membranes, in chloroplasts the thylakoid membranes.
items.misconception: Photosystems float freely in the stroma or cytoplasm, like enzymes in solution.
items.why: Chloroplast diagrams often show chlorophyll as a green colour filling the organelle, and the light-dependent reactions are described as happening 'in the chloroplast' without saying where. Photosystems are embedded in membranes, together with the electron carriers and ATP synthase, because their function depends on passing electrons to neighbouring membrane proteins and on pumping protons across the membrane.
items.specStatementText: A photosystem is an array of pigments around one reaction centre
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which pigment molecules in a photosystem emit excited electrons?
items.correct: Only the special chlorophyll at the reaction centre; the other pigments pass the energy they absorb to it.
items.misconception: Every pigment molecule in the photosystem emits its own excited electron to the electron carriers.
items.why: The guide describes photosystems as arrays that 'generate and emit excited electrons', and students apply the description to every molecule in the array. Pigment molecules in the array absorb photons and pass the excitation energy from molecule to molecule to the reaction centre. Only the reaction-centre chlorophyll emits an electron, to an acceptor in the membrane.
items.specStatementText: A photosystem is an array of pigments around one reaction centre
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which organisms first released oxygen into the Earth's atmosphere?
items.correct: Cyanobacteria, more than two billion years ago, long before land plants evolved.
items.misconception: Atmospheric oxygen comes from plants, so oxygen levels did not rise until plants evolved on land.
items.why: Photosynthesis is associated almost exclusively with plants, and rainforests are described as 'the lungs of the planet'. Photolysis in photosystem II evolved in the ancestors of cyanobacteria. Their oxygen oxidized the oceans and then accumulated in the atmosphere more than a billion years before plants colonised land.
items.specStatementText: Photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In which direction are protons pumped in the thylakoid, and where is ATP made?
items.correct: Protons are pumped from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen; they flow back into the stroma through ATP synthase, so ATP is released on the stroma side.
items.misconception: Protons are pumped into the stroma and flow back into the thylakoid lumen, where ATP is made.
items.why: In the mitochondrion protons are pumped out of the matrix and flow back into it, and ATP is made in the matrix; students assume the chloroplast works the same way round and so put ATP inside the thylakoid. In chloroplasts the thylakoid lumen is the compartment that fills with protons. The gradient drives protons out through ATP synthase into the stroma, where ATP is released for use in the Calvin cycle.
items.specStatementText: Chemiosmosis in thylakoids makes ATP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the electrons in cyclic photophosphorylation come from, and what does it produce?
items.correct: From photosystem I, to which they return via the carriers; it produces ATP only, with no reduced NADP and no oxygen.
items.misconception: Cyclic photophosphorylation uses both photosystems, or starts with photosystem II, and produces reduced NADP and oxygen as well as ATP.
items.why: The non-cyclic pathway is taught first and in more detail, and students assume the cyclic version is a loop of the same pathway rather than a separate route from photosystem I. In cyclic photophosphorylation the excited electron emitted by photosystem I is passed to the chain of carriers and back to photosystem I. Protons are pumped and ATP is made, but photosystem II, photolysis and NADP are not involved. In non-cyclic photophosphorylation the electrons come from photosystem II.
items.specStatementText: Chemiosmosis in thylakoids makes ATP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is it the presence of protons in the stroma that makes ATP synthase work?
items.correct: No. ATP synthase is driven by protons flowing through it down a concentration gradient from the thylakoid lumen to the stroma.
items.misconception: ATP synthase just needs protons to reach it, so anything that gets protons into the stroma faster makes more ATP.
items.why: Students picture protons as a fuel that ATP synthase 'uses', rather than as the flow down a gradient that turns the enzyme. Without a gradient there is no net flow through ATP synthase and no ATP is made, however many protons are present. That is why an uncoupler that lets protons leak across the membrane stops ATP synthesis.
items.specStatementText: Chemiosmosis in thylakoids makes ATP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is Rubisco used up when it fixes carbon dioxide?
items.correct: No. Like any enzyme it is released unchanged and catalyses the reaction again.
items.misconception: Rubisco is consumed each time it fixes a molecule of carbon dioxide, so large amounts must be made continuously.
items.why: The 'enzymes are used up' misconception from earlier study resurfaces when students look for a reason why so much of one enzyme is needed. Rubisco is a catalyst and is not consumed. High concentrations are needed because each molecule works slowly, not because molecules are lost.
items.specStatementText: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is carbon dioxide an abundant gas in the air?
items.correct: No. It makes up only about 0.04% of the atmosphere, which is one reason Rubisco is not effective and must be present at high concentration.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is one of the main gases in the air, so plants have plenty of it to fix.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is discussed so often in the context of climate change that students overestimate its concentration. The low concentration of carbon dioxide (about 400 parts per million) means that Rubisco, which has a low affinity for carbon dioxide, works well below its maximum rate. This is why carbon dioxide concentration is so often the limiting factor of photosynthesis and why carbon dioxide enrichment increases plant growth.
items.specStatementText: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does carbon fixation by Rubisco require ATP?
items.correct: No. ATP is used later, to convert glycerate 3-phosphate into triose phosphate and to regenerate RuBP.
items.misconception: Attaching carbon dioxide to RuBP needs an input of energy, so Rubisco uses ATP.
items.why: Students know the Calvin cycle uses ATP and assume the 'main' step, fixing the carbon, must be where it is spent. The carboxylation of RuBP by Rubisco needs no ATP or reduced NADP. ATP and reduced NADP are used to reduce glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate, and ATP alone is used to regenerate RuBP.
items.specStatementText: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is carbon dioxide reduced by hydrogen as soon as it enters the Calvin cycle?
items.correct: No. Carbon dioxide is first attached to RuBP by Rubisco, forming glycerate 3-phosphate; reduction with reduced NADP happens in the next step.
items.misconception: The first step is to add hydrogen from reduced NADP to carbon dioxide, so Rubisco's job is to reduce carbon dioxide.
items.why: The SL description 'conversion of carbon dioxide to glucose using hydrogen obtained by splitting water' suggests that hydrogen is added to carbon dioxide directly. Rubisco carboxylates RuBP; it does not reduce anything. The carbon enters as part of glycerate 3-phosphate, which is then reduced to triose phosphate using reduced NADP and ATP.
items.specStatementText: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is ATP needed in the light-independent reactions?
items.correct: Yes. ATP is used to convert glycerate 3-phosphate into triose phosphate and to regenerate RuBP.
items.misconception: Reduced NADP supplies all the energy for the Calvin cycle; ATP from the light-dependent reactions is not needed there.
items.why: Students think of the Calvin cycle as 'the reduction stage' and attach only the reducing agent to it, or think ATP is made for use elsewhere in the cell. The Calvin cycle uses both products of the light-dependent reactions: reduced NADP as the source of hydrogen for reduction and ATP as the source of energy and phosphate, in the reduction of glycerate 3-phosphate and again in the regeneration of RuBP.
items.specStatementText: Glycerate 3-phosphate is reduced to triose phosphate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a further molecule of carbon dioxide added at each step of the Calvin cycle?
items.correct: No. Carbon dioxide is added only once per turn, by Rubisco; the conversion of glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate is a reduction, not a carboxylation.
items.misconception: Triose phosphate is made by adding another carbon dioxide to glycerate 3-phosphate, so the carbon chain grows at each step.
items.why: Students expect the cycle to build glucose by adding one carbon at a time, and do not notice that glycerate 3-phosphate and triose phosphate both have three carbons. Glycerate 3-phosphate and triose phosphate are both three-carbon compounds. The conversion between them changes the molecule's oxidation state, using reduced NADP and ATP, without adding carbon.
items.specStatementText: Glycerate 3-phosphate is reduced to triose phosphate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many molecules of triose phosphate are formed for each molecule of carbon dioxide fixed?
items.correct: Two, because fixing one carbon dioxide onto a five-carbon RuBP gives two three-carbon glycerate 3-phosphates, each reduced to one triose phosphate.
items.misconception: One carbon dioxide gives one glycerate 3-phosphate and therefore one triose phosphate.
items.why: Students count the carbon dioxide molecules going in and the product molecules coming out as if they matched one to one, forgetting that RuBP contributes five carbons. One RuBP (5C) + one CO2 (1C) gives two glycerate 3-phosphate (2 × 3C), so two triose phosphates per carbon dioxide fixed. Making one glucose (6C) requires six carbon dioxides and produces twelve triose phosphates.
items.specStatementText: Five triose phosphates rebuild three RuBP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: From which compound is RuBP regenerated?
items.correct: From triose phosphate: five triose phosphates are converted into three RuBP using ATP.
items.misconception: RuBP is regenerated from glycerate 3-phosphate, so all the triose phosphate made is free to leave the cycle and make glucose.
items.why: Glycerate 3-phosphate is the first product after fixation, and students place the branch point of the cycle there rather than at triose phosphate. Glycerate 3-phosphate is reduced to triose phosphate first. Triose phosphate is the branch point: most of it (five-sixths) regenerates RuBP and the rest leaves the cycle.
items.specStatementText: Five triose phosphates rebuild three RuBP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the nitrogen in a plant's amino acids come from?
items.correct: From nitrate or ammonium ions absorbed from the soil; plants cannot fix nitrogen gas.
items.misconception: Plants fix nitrogen from the air in the Calvin cycle, in the same way as they fix carbon dioxide.
items.why: The word 'fixation' is used for both carbon and nitrogen, and students merge the two processes into one. Only carbon is fixed in the Calvin cycle. Nitrogen enters the plant as nitrate or ammonium ions from the soil (nitrogen gas is fixed only by certain bacteria) and is combined with carbon skeletons derived from Calvin cycle intermediates to make amino acids.
items.specStatementText: Every carbon compound in the plant traces back to the Calvin cycle
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is chlorophyll a reactant that is used up in photosynthesis?
items.correct: No. Chlorophyll absorbs light and is left unchanged; it contributes no atoms to glucose.
items.misconception: Chlorophyll is consumed in photosynthesis and its atoms end up in glucose, which is why it is written in the equation.
items.why: Chlorophyll is written above the arrow of the word equation alongside 'light', and students treat everything on the equation as a reactant. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and passes the energy on; it is not consumed. The atoms of glucose come from carbon dioxide and from the hydrogen of water.
items.specStatementText: Carbon dioxide plus water gives glucose, with water supplying the hydrogen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which distance goes on top when calculating Rf?
items.correct: The distance from the origin to the centre of the pigment spot; the solvent front distance goes underneath.
items.misconception: The pigment distance is the gap between the pigment spot and the solvent front, because that shows how far the pigment 'fell behind'.
items.why: On the finished chromatogram the most visible feature of a spot is its distance below the solvent front, so students measure that gap. Rf compares how far the pigment travelled with how far the solvent travelled, both measured from the origin. A pigment near the solvent front has a high Rf close to 1, not a small one.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography separates pigments, and Rf identifies them
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the pigment that travels furthest up a chromatogram the most abundant or most important one?
items.correct: No. The distance travelled depends on the pigment's solubility in the solvent and its attraction to the stationary phase, not on its amount or its importance.
items.misconception: The most abundant or most important pigment, chlorophyll, moves furthest up the paper.
items.why: Students expect the 'main' pigment to lead, and confuse the intensity of a spot (which does reflect amount) with the distance it moves. Carotene, an orange accessory pigment present in small amounts, usually has the highest Rf; the chlorophylls, although more abundant, travel less far. Pigments are identified by colour and Rf, not by assumptions about abundance.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography separates pigments, and Rf identifies them
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is light stored inside a plant?
items.correct: No. The energy of absorbed light is immediately transformed, first into the energy of an excited electron and then into chemical energy in ATP, reduced NADP and carbon compounds.
items.misconception: Plants store sunlight inside their leaves and release it later.
items.why: Phrases such as 'plants store the sun's energy' and 'food is stored sunlight' are taken literally, as if light itself were kept. Light cannot be stored. When a pigment absorbs a photon an electron is excited, and the energy is passed on and converted into chemical energy; it is chemical energy, not light, that is stored in carbon compounds.
items.specStatementText: Pigments absorb only certain wavelengths, exciting electrons
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In an experiment in which the temperature is fixed at 25 °C while the lamp is moved, is temperature the independent variable?
items.correct: No. Temperature is a controlled variable because it is kept constant; the independent variable is the one that is changed, the lamp distance.
items.misconception: A variable that the experimenter sets at a chosen value is the independent variable, so a fixed temperature is 'independent'.
items.why: Both the independent variable and the controlled variables are decided by the experimenter, and students pick the one that has a definite number attached to it. The independent variable is the one deliberately varied between trials. Variables that the experimenter fixes at one value throughout are controlled variables.
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a hypothesis just a guess?
items.correct: No. It is a provisional explanation based on theory or on existing evidence, framed so that it can be tested.
items.misconception: A hypothesis is simply a guess about what will happen; it does not need any basis in theory or evidence, because testing is all that matters.
items.why: The phrase 'educated guess' is used loosely in school science, and the 'educated' part is forgotten. Hypotheses are provisional explanations, based either on theories or on evidence from experiments already carried out, and they require repeated testing. A prediction about the result of an experiment follows from the hypothesis but is not the hypothesis itself.
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the variable that is measured carefully the controlled variable?
items.correct: No. The measured variable is the dependent variable; controlled variables are those held constant so they cannot affect the result.
items.misconception: The controlled variable is the one the experimenter measures and monitors most carefully, because that is the one they are 'controlling'.
items.why: In everyday speech to control something is to keep a close check on it, and the dependent variable is the one that is measured and recorded most carefully. A controlled variable is kept the same across all treatments (temperature, light, watering). The dry mass is the dependent variable, measured to find the effect of the independent variable.
items.specStatementText: Growing plants in extra carbon dioxide to predict the future
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does warmer water contain more dissolved carbon dioxide for an aquatic plant to use?
items.correct: No. The solubility of gases falls as temperature rises, so warm water holds less dissolved carbon dioxide; in practicals the carbon dioxide is supplied as hydrogencarbonate solution so that its concentration can be held constant.
items.misconception: Warm water dissolves more carbon dioxide, just as it dissolves more sugar or salt, so a plant in a warmer tank has more carbon dioxide available.
items.why: Students generalise from solids: sugar and salt dissolve faster and in larger amounts in hot water, and the same rule is assumed to hold for gases. Gases behave the opposite way: their solubility falls as temperature rises, which is why a warm fizzy drink goes flat. In a limiting-factor experiment the temperature is varied while the carbon dioxide concentration is held constant with hydrogencarbonate solution, so that the effect of temperature on the enzyme-catalysed reactions is isolated.
items.specStatementText: Testing how limiting factors change the rate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
